old_rewritten_text:
She was so caught up in admiring those soft blue eyes, chatting and listening, and coming up with all these plans in between, that the evening flew by at an incredible rate. Before she knew it, the supper table, which always marked the end of these gatherings, was all set and ready, and had been moved to the fireplace. With an enthusiasm that went beyond her usual eagerness to do everything well and with attention to detail, and with the genuine warmth of someone who was thrilled with her own ideas, she took charge of the meal, offering and recommending the minced chicken and scalloped oysters with a persistence that she knew would be appreciated by their guests, given the early hour and their polite reservations.

On occasions like this, poor Mr. Woodhouse's feelings were torn. He loved the tradition of laying out a spread, as it had been the custom in his youth, but his conviction that suppers were unhealthy made him regret seeing any food being served. While his hospitality would have welcomed their visitors to everything, his concern for their well-being made him worry that they would overeat.

All he could wholeheartedly recommend was a small bowl of thin gruel, similar to his own. However, as the ladies were comfortably enjoying the nicer dishes, he might suggest, 'Mrs. Bates, why don't you try one of these eggs? A soft-boiled egg isn't unhealthy. Serle is an expert at boiling eggs, and I wouldn't recommend anyone else's. But don't worry, they're very small, as you can see - one of our small eggs won't hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a little bit of tart - just a very little bit. We only have apple tarts, and you don't have to worry about unhealthy preserves here. I wouldn't advise the custard, though. Mrs. Goddard, would you like half a glass of wine? Just a small half-glass, mixed with water? I don't think it could disagree with you.'

Emma let her father talk, but she made sure their visitors were well taken care of in a much more satisfying way. That evening, she took particular pleasure in seeing them off happy. Miss Smith was just as happy as Emma had intended. As a prominent figure in Highbury, Miss Woodhouse's introduction had caused Miss Smith both excitement and nerves, but the kind and grateful young girl left with highly gratified feelings, delighted with the friendly way Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and even shaken hands with her before leaving.

Harriet Smith soon became a regular at Hartfield. Emma, being quick and decisive, wasted no time in inviting her, encouraging her to visit often, and as they spent more time together, their mutual satisfaction grew. Emma had initially seen Harriet as a potential walking companion, which was something she had been missing since Mrs. Weston's departure. Her father rarely ventured beyond the shrubbery, where two paths were enough for his daily walks, regardless of the season. Since Mrs. Weston's loss, Emma had been looking for someone to share these walks with, and Harriet seemed like the perfect companion.

The list she made when she was only fourteen - I remember thinking it showed her judgment in such a good light that I kept it for a while. I'm sure she could make a great list now, but I've given up expecting her to stick to any kind of steady reading routine. Emma will never commit to anything that requires effort and patience, or that makes her use her common sense over her imagination. Where Miss Taylor couldn't motivate her, I'm sure Harriet Smith won't be able to either. You could never get her to read as much as you wanted her to, no matter how hard you tried."

"I'm sure," Mrs. Weston replied with a smile, "that I thought that back then, but since we've been apart, I don't remember Emma ever not doing something I asked her to do."

"It's not worth bringing up a memory like that," Mr. Knightley said, feeling a bit emotional, and for a moment, he didn't say anything else. "But I, who haven't been blinded by personal feelings, still have to see, hear, and remember the truth. Emma has been spoiled because she's always been the smartest person in her family. At ten years old, she could already answer questions that her sister couldn't at seventeen. She's always been quick-witted and confident, while her sister Isabella has been slow and uncertain. Since she was twelve, Emma has been in charge of the house and everyone in it. When her mother passed away, she lost the only person who could have kept her in check. Emma inherited her mother's talents, and she would have benefited from being under her guidance."

"I would have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, if I had to rely on your recommendation if I had left the Woodhouse family and needed a new job. I don't think you would have said anything good about me to anyone. I'm sure you always thought I wasn't suited for the role I had."

"Yes," he said with a smile. "You're better off where you are now. You're a great wife, but you wouldn't have made a good governess. However, while you were at Hartfield, you were learning how to be a good wife. You might not have been able to give Emma the best education possible, but you were learning from her how to submit to someone else's will and do as you're told. If Weston had asked me to recommend a wife for him, I would have definitely suggested Miss Taylor."

"Thank you," she said. "It won't be hard to be a good wife to someone like Mr. Weston."

"Why, to be honest, I think you might be wasting your potential with him. With your disposition to be patient, there might not be anything that tests your patience. We won't give up hope, though. Maybe Weston will become grumpy because he's too comfortable, or his son might cause him trouble."

"I hope that's not the case," she said. "It's unlikely. No, Mr. Knightley, don't predict problems from that direction."

"I'm not doing that," he said. "I'm just mentioning possibilities. I don't claim to have Emma's talent for predicting the future. I hope with all my heart that the young man will have Mr. Weston's good qualities and the Churchills' wealth. But Harriet Smith - I haven't even started talking about her. I think she's the worst possible companion for Emma.

I've always thought it was a pretty unwise friendship, said Mr. Knightley after a moment, though I've kept my thoughts to myself until now. But I can see that it's going to be really bad for Harriet. You're going to give her a inflated sense of her own beauty and what she deserves, and soon nobody will be good enough for her. When vanity takes over a weak mind, it causes all sorts of problems. It's easy for a young woman to set her expectations too high. Harriet Smith might not get as many marriage proposals as she thinks, even though she's a very attractive girl. Intelligent men don't want silly wives. Men from good families wouldn't want to marry someone with such an uncertain background, and most sensible men would be afraid of the trouble and embarrassment they might face when the truth about her parents comes out. If she marries Robert Martin, she'll be safe, respected, and happy for the rest of her life. But if you encourage her to aim high and expect to marry someone rich and important, she might end up living with Mrs. Goddard forever, or at least until she gets desperate and settles for someone like the old writing teacher's son.

We clearly disagree on this, Mr. Knightley, so there's no point in discussing it further. We'll just make each other angrier. As for me allowing her to marry Robert Martin, it's impossible - she's already turned him down, and so firmly that I don't think he'll ask again. She'll have to live with the consequences of rejecting him, whatever they may be. And as for the rejection itself, I won't pretend I didn't influence her a little, but there wasn't much for me or anyone else to do. He doesn't look very appealing, and his manner is off-putting, so even if she was ever interested in him, she's not now. I can imagine that before she met anyone better, she might have tolerated him. He's the brother of her friends, and he tried to win her over, and since she hadn't met anyone better at the time, she might not have found him unpleasant when she was at Abbey-Mill. But things are different now. She knows what real gentlemen are like, and only someone with a gentleman's education and manners has a chance with Harriet.

That's nonsense, complete and utter nonsense, exclaimed Mr. Knightley. Robert Martin's manners are sensible, sincere, and good-natured, and his mind has a true gentility that Harriet Smith can't even understand.

Emma didn't respond and tried to look cheerful and unbothered, but she was actually feeling uncomfortable and wanted him to leave.

And he's a really smart boy, too. They're all incredibly smart, and they have so many charming ways. They'll come and stand by my chair, and say, 'Grandpa, can you give me a piece of string?' and once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives are only for grown-ups. I think their father is too tough on them a lot of the time."

"He seems tough to you," said Emma, "because you're so gentle yourself, but if you could compare him to other dads, you wouldn't think he's that tough. He wants his boys to be active and healthy, and if they misbehave, he can give them a firm talk now and then, but he's a loving father - Mr. John Knightley is definitely a loving father. The kids all love him."

"And then their uncle comes in and tosses them up in the air in a way that's a bit scary!"

"But they love it, Dad. There's nothing they enjoy more. It's so much fun for them that if their uncle didn't make them take turns, whoever started would never let the other one have a go."

"I just don't get it."

"That's how it is for all of us, Dad. Half the world can't understand what the other half enjoys."

Later that morning, just as the girls were about to separate to get ready for their regular 4 pm dinner, the star of this amazing charade walked in again. Harriet turned away, but Emma could greet him with a smile, and her quick eye soon picked up on the fact that he was aware of having made a move - of having taken a chance - and she thought he was there to see how it would play out. His main reason for coming, though, was to ask if Mr. Woodhouse's plans for the evening could go ahead without him, or if he was needed at Hartfield. If he was needed, everything else would have to be put on hold, but otherwise, his friend Cole had been going on and on about him coming over for dinner - had made such a big deal about it - that he had promised to come, depending on the circumstances.

Emma thanked him, but couldn't let him disappoint his friend on their account; her father was counting on him for his game. He asked again, and she said no again, and he seemed about to leave when she picked up the paper from the table and handed it back to him -

"Hey, here's the charade you were kind enough to leave with us; thanks for letting us see it. We loved it so much that I've added it to Miss Smith's collection. I hope your friend won't mind. Of course, I only copied the first eight lines."

Mr. Elton didn't seem to know what to say. He looked a bit unsure - a bit confused; said something about "honour", glanced at Emma and at Harriet, and then, seeing the book open on the table, picked it up and examined it very closely. To ease the awkward moment, Emma said with a smile,

"You'll have to apologize to your friend for me, but such a great charade can't be kept to just one or two people. He can be sure that every woman will love it as long as he writes with such charm.

You're doing the right thing,” she said. “We'll make your apologies to Mr. and Mrs. Weston.”

But she had barely spoken when her brother offered Mr. Elton a ride in his car, saying that if the weather was the only thing holding him back, he'd be happy to give him a lift. To her surprise, Mr. Elton accepted the offer with evident satisfaction. It was a done deal; Mr. Elton was going, and his face had never looked happier. His smile was stronger than ever, and his eyes sparkled with excitement as he glanced at her.

“Well,” she thought to herself, “this is really strange. After I managed to get him to stay behind, he chooses to go out and leave Harriet alone when she's not feeling well. It's just weird. But I think a lot of men, especially single guys, have this thing about going out to dinner. It's like, a top priority for them - it's up there with their jobs, their social status, and their sense of duty. So, anything else takes a backseat, and that must be what's going on with Mr. Elton. He's a great guy, really likable and charming, and he's clearly into Harriet, but he just can't resist a dinner invitation. It's like, love is a weird thing - he can see how smart and funny Harriet is, but he won't even skip dinner to spend time with her.”

Soon after, Mr. Elton left, and she had to admit that there was something endearing about the way he mentioned Harriet when he said goodbye. The way he spoke, the tone of his voice, it all seemed so sincere, especially when he promised to stop by Mrs. Goddard's to check in on Harriet and hopefully bring back some good news. He sighed and smiled as he left, and it was hard not to be impressed.

After a few minutes of silence, John Knightley spoke up. “I've never seen anyone try so hard to be charming as Mr. Elton. It's like, he's putting in a lot of effort to make a good impression, especially when there are women around. With men, he's fine, totally normal and down-to-earth, but when he's around women, it's like he's performing or something.”

“Mr. Elton's manners aren't perfect,” Emma replied, “but when someone's trying their best to be nice, you've got to give them some credit. And when someone's doing their best with what they've got, that's more impressive than someone who's just coasting on their natural talent. Mr. Elton's just so friendly and well-meaning that you can't help but like him.”

John Knightley nodded, a hint of a smile on his face. “Yeah, he seems to have a lot of good feelings towards you, Emma.”

Her eyes widened in surprise. “Me? You think Mr. Elton's interested in me?”

John Knightley leaned in, a sly glint in his eye. “Well, it's crossed my mind, and even if it hasn't occurred to you before, maybe you should consider it now.”

The idea was laughable. “Mr. Elton in love with me? That's just ridiculous.”

John Knightley's expression turned serious. “I'm not saying it's true, but you should think about it and maybe adjust your behavior accordingly. I think you've been kind of encouraging him, Emma.”

I made my way along the path as quickly as possible. After crossing a ditch that I knew was close to the Battery, I climbed up the mound on the other side and saw a man sitting in front of me. His back was turned to me, and he had his arms folded, nodding forward as he struggled to stay awake.

I thought he would appreciate it if I surprised him with his breakfast, so I approached him quietly and touched his shoulder. He immediately jumped up, but to my surprise, it wasn't the same man - it was someone else.

This new man was also dressed in coarse grey clothing, had a large iron shackle on his leg, and was lame, hoarse, and cold, just like the first man. However, he had a different face and was wearing a flat, broad-brimmed hat. I took all of this in quickly, as I only had a moment to react. He cursed at me, swung at me with a weak, clumsy blow that missed me and almost knocked him off balance, and then he ran into the mist, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

'It's the young man,' I thought, feeling my heart racing as I realized who it was. I probably would have felt a pang of fear if I had known what to expect.

Soon after, I arrived at the Battery, and there was the original man, hugging himself and limping back and forth as if he had been doing it all night, waiting for me. He was extremely cold, and I was worried that he might collapse in front of me at any moment. His eyes looked hungry, and when I handed him the file and he put it down on the grass, I thought he might try to eat it if he hadn't seen the food in my bundle. This time, he didn't turn me upside down to get to my belongings, but instead let me stay upright while I opened the bundle and emptied my pockets.

'What's in the bottle, boy?' he asked.

'Brandy,' I replied.

He was already eating the mincemeat in a frantic, hurried manner, but he stopped to take a swig of the liquor. He was shivering so violently that it was a struggle for him to keep the bottle steady without biting it.

'I think you have a bad case of the flu,' I said.

'I think you're right, boy,' he agreed.

'It's not good around here,' I told him. 'You've been lying out in the marshes, and they're notorious for being unhealthy. You're probably going to get rheumatism too.'

'I'll eat my breakfast before I die from it,' he said. 'I'd do that even if I was going to be hanged from the gallows over there right afterwards. I'll shake off the chills, I'm sure of it.'

He was devouring the mincemeat, meat, bread, cheese, and pork pie all at once, staring suspiciously at the mist surrounding us and frequently stopping to listen, even stopping mid-chew.

The sergeant downed his drink again and seemed ready for another. I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook, in his eagerness to play host, appeared to forget that he had given the wine as a gift, but took the bottle from Mrs. Joe and got all the credit for pouring it for everyone in a show of friendliness. Even I got some. He was so generous with the wine that he even called for the other bottle and passed it around with the same liberality when the first one was empty.

As I watched them all gathered around the forge, having a great time, I thought about how my fugitive friend on the marshes had added a lot of excitement to our dinner. They hadn't been having nearly as much fun before he showed up and caused such a commotion. Now, with everyone eagerly waiting for the two escapees to be caught, and the bellows seeming to roar with anticipation, the fire blazing with intensity, the smoke rushing away as if in pursuit, Joe hammering and clinking away, and all the dark shadows on the wall seeming to shake with menace as the flames rose and fell, and the red-hot sparks dropped and died out, the pale afternoon outside seemed to have grown even paler in my young imagination, as if it felt sorry for the poor guys.

Finally, Joe finished his task, and the noise stopped. As Joe put on his coat, he mustered up the courage to suggest that some of us should go with the soldiers and see how the hunt turned out. Mr. Pumblechook and Mr. Hubble declined, saying they'd rather stay behind and enjoy their pipes and the ladies' company. But Mr. Wopsle said he'd go if Joe would. Joe agreed and said he'd take me along if Mrs. Joe gave her okay. I'm sure we wouldn't have been allowed to go if Mrs. Joe hadn't been curious about what would happen and how it would all end. As it was, she just said, 'If you bring the boy back with his head blown off by a gunshot, don't expect me to put it back together again.'

The sergeant politely said goodbye to the ladies and parted ways with Mr. Pumblechook like they were old friends, although I doubt he had as much respect for Mr. Pumblechook when he was sober. His men picked up their rifles and fell in line. Mr. Wopsle, Joe, and I were strictly told to stay in the back and not say a word once we reached the marshes. When we were all outside in the cold air and heading towards our destination, I whispered to Joe, 'I hope we don't find them,' and Joe whispered back, 'I'd pay a shilling if they'd just run away, Pip.'

We didn't meet any stragglers from the village, since the weather was cold and gloomy, the path was dreary, the ground was uneven, and darkness was approaching. The people had warm fires going at home and were staying indoors. A few faces appeared at glowing windows and watched us leave, but no one came out to join us. We passed the signpost and continued straight on to the churchyard. We were stopped for a few minutes by a signal from the sergeant, while a few of his men spread out among the graves and checked the porch.

Go, Pip.” I followed Estella down, and she placed the candle where we had found it. Until she opened the side door, I had assumed it was nighttime. “Good. You should try to meet him at his own home. The way will be cleared for you, and you can see his son first, who is in London. When will you come to London?”

I said (glancing at Joe, who stood looking on, motionless), that I supposed I could come right away.

“First,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you should get some new clothes to wear, and they shouldn't be your work clothes. How about this day next week? You'll need some money. Shall I leave you twenty guineas?”

He pulled out a long wallet with complete calmness, counted out the money on the table, and pushed it over to me. This was the first time he had moved his leg from the chair. He sat astride the chair after pushing the money over, swinging his wallet and eyeing Joe.

“Well, Joseph Gargery? You look stunned,” Mr. Jaggers said.

“I am,” said Joe, in a very decisive manner.

“It was understood that you didn't want anything for yourself, remember?” Mr. Jaggers asked.

“It was understood,” said Joe. “And it still is. And it always will be that way.”

“But what,” said Mr. Jaggers, swinging his wallet, “if my instructions were to give you a gift as compensation?”

“As compensation for what?” Joe demanded.

“For the loss of Pip's services,” Mr. Jaggers replied.

I discovered that Wemmick was the clerk in the adjacent room. As he stepped out, another clerk was summoned from upstairs to take his place, and I accompanied him into the street after bidding farewell to my guardian. We encountered a new group of people lingering outside, but Wemmick effortlessly navigated through them by stating calmly yet firmly, 'I assure you, it's pointless; he won't engage with any of you,' and we soon cleared a path and continued on our way side by side.

As we walked, I took the opportunity to observe Mr. Wemmick in the daylight. I found him to be a somewhat austere man, slightly below average height, with a wooden face whose features seemed to have been roughly hewn with a blunt instrument. There were a few marks on his face that could have been dimples if the material had been more pliable and the tool more refined, but instead, they appeared as mere indentations. The instrument had attempted to create a few of these decorative touches above his nose but had abandoned the effort without smoothing them out. I surmised that he was a bachelor, given the worn state of his linen, and he seemed to have experienced numerous losses, as evidenced by the multiple mourning rings he wore, in addition to a brooch depicting a lady and a weeping willow beside a tomb with an urn. I also noticed that several rings and seals hung from his watch-chain, as if he were heavily burdened with memories of departed friends. His eyes sparkled - small, sharp, and black - and his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. To the best of my knowledge, he had possessed these features for forty to fifty years.

'Had you never been to London before?' Mr. Wemmick inquired of me.

'No,' I replied.

'I, too, was once new to this city,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'It's strange to think about now.'

'Are you well acquainted with London now?' I asked.

'Oh, yes,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'I'm familiar with its ways.'

'Is it a particularly wicked place?' I asked, more out of a desire to make conversation than to gain insight.

'You can be deceived, robbed, or murdered in London,' he said. 'However, there are plenty of people elsewhere who would do the same to you.'

'If there's ill will between you and them,' I added, attempting to soften the statement.

'Oh, I don't know about ill will,' Mr. Wemmick responded. 'There isn't much of that about. They'll do it if there's something to be gained.'

'That makes it worse,' I said.

'Do you think so?' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'I'd say it's much the same.'

He wore his hat at the back of his head and gazed straight ahead, walking with a self-assured air as if nothing in the streets warranted his attention. His mouth seemed to be perpetually frozen in a mechanical smile, giving him a somewhat artificial appearance. We had reached the top of Holborn Hill before I realized that this was merely a facade, and he wasn't actually smiling at all.

'Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket resides?' I asked Mr. Wemmick.

'Yes,' he replied, nodding in a particular direction. 'He lives in Hammersmith, to the west of London.'

'Is that far?'

Who's the Spider?” I was asked.

“The spider?” I replied.

“The guy with the messy, sulky demeanor,” the person clarified.

“That's Bentley Drummle,” I said; “the one with the delicate face is Startop.”

My companion didn't seem to care about Startop and instead focused on Drummle, saying, “Bentley Drummle, that's his name? I like the look of that guy.”

He immediately started talking to Drummle, undeterred by Drummle's brief and reserved responses. In fact, Drummle's reserved nature seemed to encourage my companion to try to get more out of him. As I watched the two of them, the housekeeper appeared with the first course for dinner.

She was a woman who appeared to be around forty, although I might have underestimated her age. She was tall and slender, extremely pale, with large, faded eyes and a lot of long, flowing hair. I couldn't help but notice that her lips were parted, as if she were out of breath, and her face had a strange, fluttery expression. It reminded me of the faces I had seen in a production of Macbeth at the theater a night or two before, which seemed to be disturbed by some kind of intense, fiery energy.

The housekeeper set the dish down, discreetly touched my guardian's arm to let him know that dinner was ready, and then disappeared. We took our seats at the round table, with my guardian sitting between Drummle and Startop. The housekeeper had prepared an excellent dish of fish, which was followed by a delicious joint of mutton and then a superb bird. Our host provided us with a wide range of sauces, wines, and other accompaniments, all of which were of the highest quality. He used a dumbwaiter to serve us, and when each dish had made its way around the table, he would put it back and bring out the next one. He also made sure we had clean plates, knives, and forks for each course, and he would drop the used ones into baskets on the floor beside his chair. The housekeeper was the only other person who attended to us, and she was the one who brought out each dish. Every time I saw her, I was struck by her resemblance to the faces I had seen in the theater production.

Because the housekeeper's appearance was so striking, and because Wemmick had prepared me for her, I found myself paying close attention to her. I noticed that whenever she was in the room, she kept a close eye on my guardian, and when she was serving him, she would hesitate before removing her hands from the dish, as if she were afraid he would call her back. It seemed to me that she wanted him to speak to her when she was near, if he had anything to say. I also thought I detected a sense of awareness in my guardian's manner, as if he knew she was watching him and was intentionally keeping her in a state of suspense.

Dinner was a lively and enjoyable affair, and although my guardian didn't seem to be driving the conversation, I knew that he had a way of drawing out our weaker qualities. He had a knack for getting us to reveal more about ourselves than we might have intended.

The gusts had been so intense that they had ripped the lead off the roofs of tall buildings in town, and in the countryside, trees had been uprooted and windmill sails had been torn away. There were also grim reports of shipwrecks and fatalities coming in from the coast. The violent wind had been accompanied by heavy rain, and the day that had just ended as I sat down to read had been the worst of all. 

Since then, changes have been made to that part of the Temple, and it no longer has the same isolated feel it had back then, nor is it as exposed to the river. We lived in the top apartment, and the wind rushing up the river shook the building that night, sounding like cannon fire or waves crashing against the shore. When the rain hit the windows, I thought, looking up at them as they swayed, that I could have imagined myself in a lighthouse battered by a storm. Occasionally, the smoke would pour down the chimney as if it couldn't stand to go out into such a night, and when I opened the doors and looked down the stairs, the staircase lights had been extinguished. When I covered my face with my hands and peeked through the dark windows - it was impossible to open them even a little in the face of such strong wind and rain - I saw that the lamps in the courtyard had also been blown out, and the lamps on the bridges and the shore were swaying, and the coal fires in the barges on the river were being swept away by the wind like red-hot sparks in the rain.

I read with my watch on the table, planning to finish my book at 11 PM. As I closed it, the sound of Saint Paul's and all the many church clocks in the city - some leading, some accompanying, some following - struck the hour. The sound was strangely distorted by the wind, and I was listening, thinking about how the wind was attacking and tearing it apart, when I heard footsteps on the stairs. 

What nervous foolishness made me jump and horribly connect it with the footsteps of my deceased sister, I don't know. It was over in a moment, and I listened again and heard the footsteps stumble as they continued up. Remembering that the staircase lights were out, I picked up my reading lamp and went out to the top of the stairs. Whoever was below had stopped when they saw my lamp, and everything was quiet.

'Is there someone down there?' I called out, looking down.

'Yes,' a voice replied from the darkness below.

'What floor are you looking for?'

'The top. Mr. Pip.'

'That's my name. Is everything okay?'

'Everything's fine,' the voice replied, and the man started coming up.

I stood with my lamp held out over the stair rail, and he slowly came into its light. It was a shaded lamp, meant to shine on a book, and its circle of light was very small, so he was only in it for a brief moment before he was out of it again. In that moment, I saw a face that was unfamiliar to me, looking up with an inexplicable air of being touched and pleased by the sight of me.

My main goal is to launch a magazine called 'The Stylus,' but it would be pointless unless I have complete control over it, without any publisher interference. To achieve this, I plan to create a journal that is entirely my own. To make this happen, I need to secure a list of at least 500 subscribers to start with; I already have nearly 200. I intend to travel to the South and West to connect with my personal and literary friends, including old college and West Point acquaintances, to see what I can accomplish. To get the necessary funds to take the first step, I plan to give a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, February 3rd, and to avoid any controversy, my topic will not be related to literature at all. I've chosen a broad subject: 'The Universe.'

Having shared the facts of the situation with you, I leave the rest to your discretion and generosity. Thank you, very gratefully,

Your friend always,
EDGAR A. POE.

old_rewritten_text: I feared that my friend's prolonged exposure to misfortune might have finally taken a toll on his sanity. Without hesitation, I decided to accompany the negro to our destination. Upon arriving at the wharf, I noticed a newly purchased scythe and three spades lying in the boat that was to take us on our journey. I turned to Jup and asked, 'What is the purpose of these tools?' He replied, 'Him syfe and spade, massa.' I pressed him for a more detailed explanation, 'Yes, I see that, but why are they here?' Jup responded, 'Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will sis pon my buying for him in de town, and de debbil's own lot of money I had to gib for 'em.' I was perplexed and asked, 'But what could your "Massa Will" possibly want with scythes and spades?' Jup's response was vague, 'Dat's more dan I know, and debbil take me if I don't b'lieve 'tis more dan he know, too. But it's all cum ob do bug.' Since I couldn't get any clear answers from Jup, whose mind seemed preoccupied with 'de bug,' I boarded the boat and we set sail. With a favorable breeze, we soon arrived at a small cove north of Fort Moultrie. A two-mile walk brought us to the hut, where we arrived around three in the afternoon. Legrand was waiting for us, his eagerness evident in his nervous demeanor, which only served to heighten my concerns about his well-being. His pale complexion and intense gaze further alarmed me. After inquiring about his health, I asked if he had managed to obtain the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——. He replied, his face flushing, 'Oh, yes, I got it from him the next morning. I would never consider parting with that _scarabæus_.' He then added, with a serious tone, 'Jupiter is right about it, you know.' I felt a sense of foreboding and asked, 'In what way?' Legrand's response was astonishing, 'In thinking it's a bug made of real gold.' He spoke with conviction, and I was shocked by his words. He continued, a triumphant smile spreading across his face, 'This bug will be my ticket to reclaiming my family's possessions. It's no wonder I treasure it. Now that Fortune has seen fit to grant it to me, I just need to use it wisely, and I'll uncover the gold it points to.' He called out to Jup, 'Jupiter, bring me that _scarabæus!_' Jup hesitated, 'What, de bug, massa? I'd rather not trouble dat bug – you mus' git him for your own self.' Legrand rose from his seat, his movements grave and deliberate, and retrieved the beetle from a glass case. The _scarabæus_ was a stunning specimen, unknown to naturalists at the time, and thus a valuable find from a scientific perspective. It had two round, black spots near one end of its back and a long one near the other. The scales glistened with a burnished gold appearance, and the insect's weight was remarkable. Considering all these factors, I couldn't help but understand why Jupiter thought it was made of gold, but I was still baffled by Legrand's agreement with this assessment.

We don't mean to cause you any harm. I promise you, as a gentleman and a Frenchman, that we don't intend to hurt you. I'm well aware that you're innocent of the atrocities that took place in the Rue Morgue. However, it's not possible to deny that you're somehow involved in them. From what I've already said, you must know that I have access to information about this matter that you couldn't have even imagined. The situation is this: you haven't done anything that you could have avoided, and certainly nothing that would make you guilty. You didn't even take anything when you had the chance to do so without getting caught. You have nothing to hide, and no reason to keep anything secret. On the other hand, you're bound by every principle of honor to tell us everything you know. An innocent person is currently in prison, accused of a crime that you can help us solve by identifying the real perpetrator.

The sailor had regained his composure to a great extent while Dupin was speaking, but his initial confidence was gone.

"So help me God!" he said after a brief pause. "I'll tell you everything I know about this affair, but I don't expect you to believe half of what I say. I'd be a fool if I did. Still, I'm innocent, and I'll come clean even if it kills me."

What he told us was essentially this: he had recently returned from a voyage to the Indian Archipelago. A group he was part of had landed in Borneo and ventured into the interior for a pleasure trip. He and a companion had captured an orangutan. After his companion died, the animal became his sole responsibility. After a lot of trouble caused by the orangutan's aggressive behavior during the return voyage, he finally managed to safely house it at his residence in Paris. To avoid drawing unwanted attention from his neighbors, he kept the animal secluded until it recovered from a foot injury it had sustained on the ship. His ultimate plan was to sell it.

One night, or rather early in the morning of the murder, he returned home from a night out with other sailors and found the orangutan in his bedroom, where it had broken in from a closet where it was supposed to be securely locked. The animal was sitting in front of a mirror, trying to shave itself with a razor, having apparently watched its owner do so through the keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the hands of a ferocious animal, the man was at a loss for what to do. However, he had experience calming the creature down with a whip, so he used that. As soon as the orangutan saw the whip, it jumped out of the room, down the stairs, and out a window that was unfortunately open, into the street.

The Frenchman followed in desperation; the orangutan, still holding the razor, would occasionally stop and look back at its pursuer, gesturing at him, until the Frenchman was about to catch up.

To me, this article seems to prove little beyond the author's enthusiasm. We should keep in mind that, in general, the goal of our newspapers is to create a sensation, to make a point, rather than to advance the cause of truth. The pursuit of truth only happens when it aligns with creating a sensation. An article that simply agrees with popular opinion, no matter how well-founded that opinion may be, doesn't earn any credit with the public. Most people consider someone profound only if they suggest provocative contradictions to the general idea. In both logical reasoning and literature, it's the witty, concise statement that's most immediately and universally appreciated, even though it's often of the lowest order of merit.

What I'm trying to say is that it's the combination of a catchy phrase and a dramatic idea - the notion that Marie Rogêt is still alive - rather than any real plausibility in this idea, that led L'Etoile to suggest it and made it well-received by the public. Let's examine the main points of this journal's argument, trying to avoid the confusion with which it was originally presented.

The writer's first goal is to show that, given the short time between Marie's disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, this corpse can't be Marie's. The writer wants to minimize this time interval as much as possible, which becomes an objective in itself. In the rush to achieve this, the writer jumps to assumptions right from the start. 'It's foolish to think,' the writer says, 'that if Marie was murdered, her killers could have done it quickly enough to throw her body into the river before midnight.' We immediately ask, why? Why is it foolish to think that the murder could have happened within five minutes of the girl leaving her mother's house? Why is it foolish to think that the murder could have happened at any given time of day? There have been assassinations at all hours. But if the murder had taken place at any moment between 9 am on Sunday and a quarter to midnight, there would still have been enough time to throw the body into the river before midnight. This assumption essentially means that the murder didn't happen on Sunday at all - and if we let L'Etoile assume this, we might as well let them assume anything. The paragraph starting 'It's foolish to think that the murder, etc.' may have existed in the writer's mind like this: 'It's foolish to think that the murder, if it happened, could have happened quickly enough to allow the killers to throw the body into the river before midnight; it's foolish, we say, to think all this and at the same time assume that the body wasn't thrown in until after midnight' - a sentence that's inconsequential in itself but not as absurd as the one that was printed.

If my goal were simply to criticize this part of L'Etoile's argument, I could safely leave it as it is.

I did confess, but it was a lie. I confessed to get forgiveness, but now that lie weighs heavier on my heart than all my other mistakes. I hope God forgives me. Ever since I was sentenced, my confessor has been pressuring me, threatening and intimidating me until I almost started to believe I was the monster he said I was. He threatened to excommunicate me and condemn me to hell if I didn't cooperate. Dear lady, I had no one to support me; everyone saw me as a person doomed to shame and destruction. What could I do? In a moment of weakness, I agreed to a lie; and now I'm truly miserable.

She paused, crying, and then continued, 'I was horrified, my dear lady, that you would think Justine, whom your aunt had honored so much and whom you loved, was capable of a crime that only a truly evil person could commit. Dear William, my sweet child, I'll see you again in heaven, where we'll all be happy, and that gives me some comfort as I face shame and death.'

'Oh, Justine, forgive me for doubting you, even if it was just for a moment. Why did you confess? But don't cry, don't be afraid. I'll speak out, I'll prove your innocence. I'll move the hearts of your enemies with my tears and prayers. You won't die. You, my friend, my companion, my sister, can't perish on the scaffold. No, no, I couldn't survive such a terrible tragedy.'

Justine shook her head sadly. 'I'm not afraid to die,' she said. 'That fear is gone. God gives me the strength to endure the worst. I'm leaving a sad and bitter world, and if you remember me as someone who was wrongly condemned, I'm at peace with my fate. Learn from me, dear lady, to accept the will of heaven with patience.'

During this conversation, I had stepped back to a corner of the prison room, where I could hide the terrible anguish that was overwhelming me. Despair? Who dared to talk about that? The poor victim, who would soon face death, didn't feel the same deep and bitter pain that I did. I clenched my teeth and ground them together, letting out a groan that came from deep inside me. Justine noticed. When she saw who it was, she came over to me and said, 'Dear sir, you're very kind to visit me. I hope you don't think I'm guilty?'

I couldn't answer. 'No, Justine,' said Elizabeth, 'he's even more convinced of your innocence than I was. Even when he heard you had confessed, he didn't believe it.'

'I truly thank him. In these last moments, I feel grateful to those who think of me with kindness. The love and support of others mean so much to someone like me. It takes away more than half my suffering, and I feel like I can die in peace now that you and your cousin believe in my innocence.'

The poor woman tried to comfort others and herself, even in her own time of need.

I couldn't bring myself to agree with the death of any human being, but I definitely thought such a creature was unfit to be part of society. However, she was innocent. I know, I feel, she was innocent; you share my opinion, and that reassures me. Unfortunately, Victor, when lies can be so convincing, who can be certain of true happiness? I feel like I'm walking on the edge of a cliff, with thousands pushing me towards the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, and the killer is still at large, free and possibly respected. Even if I were sentenced to death for the same crimes, I wouldn't trade places with such a person.

I listened to this conversation with extreme distress. Essentially, I was the real murderer. Elizabeth saw my anguish and took my hand, saying, 'My dearest friend, you need to calm down. These events have affected me deeply, but I'm not as miserable as you are. There's a look of despair and sometimes revenge in your eyes that scares me. Dear Victor, get rid of these dark emotions. Remember the friends around you who put all their hopes in you. Have we lost the power to make you happy? As long as we love and are true to each other, here in this peaceful and beautiful land, your homeland, we can enjoy every serene blessing - what could disturb our peace?'

And couldn't words like these from the person I cherished above all else be enough to drive away the evil that lurked in my heart? Even as she spoke, I drew closer to her, as if I was afraid that at that very moment, something terrible would take her away from me.

Not even the kindness of friendship, the beauty of the earth, or the beauty of heaven could save my soul from sorrow; the very sound of love was ineffective. I was surrounded by a darkness that no positive influence could penetrate. A wounded deer dragging its weak limbs to a secluded spot to stare at the arrow that pierced it and die was similar to my situation.

Sometimes I could handle the overwhelming despair, but sometimes the intense emotions inside me drove me to seek relief through physical activity and a change of scenery. It was during one of these episodes that I suddenly left my home and headed towards the nearby Alpine valleys, seeking to forget myself and my fleeting human sorrows in the grandeur and timelessness of such landscapes. My travels took me to the valley of Chamounix, a place I had visited often during my childhood. Six years had passed since then; I was a shadow of my former self, but nothing had changed in those rugged and enduring scenes.

I started my journey on horseback and later hired a mule, as it was more sure-footed and less likely to get injured on these rough roads. The weather was nice; it was around the middle of August, nearly two months after Justine's death, a miserable time that marked the beginning of all my troubles.

Remember the friends who surround you and have placed all their hopes in you. Have we lost the ability to make you happy? “You're a monster,” I exclaimed. “How dare you come near me? Don't you fear my wrath and the punishment I'll inflict on you? Get out of here, you vile creature! Or stay, so I can crush you. Oh, if only I could destroy you and bring back the people you've brutally murdered!

“I expected you to react this way,” the creature said. “All people hate those who are suffering; how much more must I be hated, since I'm more miserable than anyone alive? Yet you, my creator, reject and despise me, your own creation, to whom you're bound by a tie that can only be broken by one of us dying. You want to kill me. How can you play with life like that? Do your duty towards me, and I'll do mine towards you and the rest of humanity. If you agree to my terms, I'll leave them and you alone; but if you refuse, I'll keep killing until death is satisfied with the blood of your remaining friends.”

“Abhorrent monster! You're a fiend! The torments of hell are too mild a punishment for your crimes. You blame me for creating you? Come on, then, so I can extinguish the life I so carelessly gave you.”

My rage was uncontrollable; I lunged at him, driven by all the feelings that can make one being want to destroy another.

He easily dodged me and said, “Calm down! Please listen to me before you act on your hatred. Haven't I suffered enough without you trying to increase my misery? Life, even if it's just a collection of pain, is precious to me, and I'll defend it. Remember, you made me stronger than you; I'm taller and more agile. But I won't fight you. I'm your creation, and I'll be gentle and obedient to my natural master if you'll just do your part, which you owe me. Oh, Frankenstein, don't be fair to everyone else and cruel to me alone, when I'm the one who deserves your justice, mercy, and love. Remember that I'm your creation; I should be your partner, but instead I'm like a fallen angel, banished from happiness for no reason. Everywhere I see people happy, and I'm the only one excluded. I was kind and good; misery turned me into a monster. Make me happy, and I'll be virtuous again.”

“Get out! I won't listen to you. There can be no connection between us; we're enemies. Leave, or let's settle this in a fight, where one of us will die.”

“How can I make you understand? Will you never look at me with kindness, your creation who's begging for your compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was once full of love and humanity; but now I'm alone, miserably alone. You, my creator, reject me; what hope can I have from other people, who owe me nothing? They shun and hate me. The desolate mountains and glaciers are my refuge. I've been wandering here for days; the ice caves, which are the only place I don't fear, are my home, and the only one that humanity doesn't deny me.”

A significant amount of time passed before I discovered one of the reasons behind the unease of this lovely family: it was poverty, and they were struggling with it in a really tough way. Their diet consisted entirely of the vegetables from their garden and the milk from one cow, which didn't produce much during the winter when its owners could barely find food to keep it alive. I believe the two younger family members often went hungry, as they would frequently give the older man food while going without themselves.

This act of kindness really moved me. At night, I had been sneaking into their storage to take some food for myself, but when I realized that this was causing the family pain, I stopped and started eating berries, nuts, and roots that I found in a nearby forest instead.

I also found another way to help the family. I noticed that the young man spent a lot of time each day collecting firewood for the family's fire, and at night, I would often take his tools and use them to bring back enough firewood to last for several days.

I remember the first time I did this, the young woman was really surprised when she opened the door in the morning and saw a big pile of wood outside. She exclaimed loudly, and the young man joined her, also looking surprised. I was happy to see that he didn't go to the forest that day, but instead spent his time fixing up the cottage and tending to the garden.

As time went on, I made an even more important discovery. I found out that these people had a way of sharing their thoughts and feelings with each other using spoken language. I realized that the words they spoke could bring joy or sadness, smiles or tears, to the people listening. This was an incredible ability, and I was eager to learn it. However, I was unable to figure it out, no matter how hard I tried. The way they pronounced their words was quick, and the words themselves didn't seem to be connected to anything tangible, so I couldn't find any clues to help me understand what they meant. But after spending several months in my hiding place, I finally started to learn the names of some common objects, like fire, milk, bread, and wood. I also learned the names of the family members: the old man was called Father, the young woman was called Sister or Agatha, and the young man was called Felix, Brother, or Son. I was thrilled when I learned what these words meant and could pronounce them myself. I picked up on a few other words, like good, dearest, and unhappy, but I still didn't fully understand what they meant.

I spent the winter this way. The family's kind nature and beauty had really grown on me, and I found myself feeling down when they were sad and happy when they were joyful.

old_rewritten_text:
They made many gestures that I didn't understand, but I could see that her presence brought happiness to the cottage, dispelling their sadness like the sun burning off the morning fog. Felix seemed especially happy and welcomed his Arabian friend with big smiles. Agatha, who was always kind, kissed the stranger's hands and pointed to her brother, making signs that seemed to mean he had been sad until she arrived. For a few hours, they all showed joy on their faces, but I didn't get what was causing it. Then I noticed that the stranger was trying to learn their language by repeating words after them, and it occurred to me that I could use the same method to learn too. The stranger picked up about twenty words in the first lesson, and although most of them were words I already knew, I still learned from the others.

As night fell, Agatha and the Arabian went to bed early. When they said their goodbyes, Felix kissed the stranger's hand and said, 'Good night, sweet Safie.' He stayed up late talking to his father, and from how often they mentioned her name, I guessed that their beautiful guest was the topic of conversation. I really wanted to understand what they were saying, so I focused all my attention on it, but it was impossible.

The next morning, Felix went to work, and after Agatha finished her usual tasks, the Arabian sat at the old man's feet and started playing the guitar. The music was so beautiful that it brought tears of sadness and joy to my eyes. She sang with a rich, flowing voice that sounded like a nightingale in the woods.

When she finished, she handed the guitar to Agatha, who at first didn't want to take it. But then she played a simple melody, singing along in a sweet voice, although it wasn't as amazing as the stranger's music. The old man seemed completely enchanted and said something that Agatha tried to explain to Safie, which seemed to mean that Agatha's music gave him great pleasure.

From then on, life went back to being peaceful, with the only difference being that joy had replaced sadness on my friends' faces. Safie was always happy and carefree, and she and I quickly improved our language skills. Within two months, I could understand most of what my friends were saying.

Meanwhile, the black earth was covered in green plants, and the banks were filled with countless flowers that smelled sweet and looked beautiful, like stars shining in the moonlight. The sun got warmer, the nights became clear and mild, and I loved taking walks at night, even though they were shorter because the sun set late and rose early. I never went out during the day, though, because I was afraid of being treated badly like I was in the first village I visited.

I spent my days focusing hard on learning the language, and I can say that I improved faster than the Arabian, who understood very little and spoke with a strong accent. I could comprehend and imitate almost every word that was spoken.

Safie told me that her mother was a Christian Arab who had been captured and enslaved by the Turks. Because of her beauty, she caught the eye of Safie's father, who married her. Safie spoke highly of her mother, who had been born free but was now forced into bondage. Despite this, she taught Safie about her Christian faith and encouraged her to strive for intellectual freedom and independence, values that were discouraged for women in Muslim societies. After her mother's death, Safie was determined to hold on to these lessons. The thought of returning to Asia and being confined to a harem, with only childish pursuits to occupy her time, was unbearable to her. She longed for the freedom to think and act for herself, and the idea of marrying a Christian and living in a country where women had more rights was incredibly appealing.

The day of the Turk's execution was set, but he escaped from prison the night before and was far away from Paris by morning. Felix had obtained passports for himself, his father, and his sister, using his father's name. He had told his father about his plan, and his father had pretended to leave on a trip, hiding with his daughter in a secluded part of the city.

Felix led the group through France to Lyons and then across the Mont Cenis pass to Leghorn, where the merchant was waiting for a chance to sneak into the Turkish territories.

Safie decided to stay with her father until he left, and during this time, the Turk renewed his promise that she would be united with Felix. Felix stayed with them, waiting for this to happen, and he enjoyed Safie's company. They communicated through an interpreter, and sometimes they just looked at each other to understand what the other was thinking. Safie would sing traditional songs from her homeland to Felix.

The Turk allowed Felix and Safie to spend time together and even encouraged their hopes of being together, but secretly, he had other plans. He didn't want his daughter to marry a Christian, but he was afraid of what Felix might do if he found out. The Turk knew that Felix could still turn him in to the authorities if he wanted to. So, he came up with a plan to keep pretending to agree to the marriage until it was no longer necessary, and then he would take Safie with him when he left. News from Paris made it easier for him to carry out his plan.

The French government was furious that the Turk had escaped, and they were doing everything they could to catch and punish the person who had helped him. Felix's plan was soon discovered, and his father and sister were thrown into prison. When Felix heard the news, it woke him up from his dream of happiness. His blind and elderly father and his kind sister were suffering in a dirty prison cell, while he was free to enjoy the company of the woman he loved.

I spent the rest of the day in my hut, consumed by a deep and overwhelming despair. My protectors had left me, and with them, the only connection I had to the world. For the first time, I felt intense anger and hatred, and I didn't try to control these emotions. Instead, I let them take over, focusing my mind on causing harm and destruction. When I thought about my friends, like the gentle De Lacey, the kind Agatha, and the beautiful Arabian, these thoughts faded away, and a wave of tears brought me some comfort. But when I remembered that they had rejected and abandoned me, my anger returned, and I was filled with a rage that I couldn't direct at any human. So, I turned my fury on inanimate objects. As night fell, I gathered various flammable materials around the cottage and, after destroying everything in the garden, I waited impatiently for the moon to set before starting my destruction.

As the night wore on, a strong wind picked up from the woods, quickly clearing the clouds from the sky. The gusts were like a powerful avalanche, and they stirred up a kind of madness in me that broke free from all reason and reflection. I lit a dry tree branch and danced around the cottage with fury, my eyes fixed on the western horizon, where the moon was about to dip below the edge. As the moon disappeared, I waved my torch, and with a loud scream, I set the straw, heath, and bushes I had collected on fire. The wind fueled the flames, and the cottage was quickly engulfed, with the fire clinging to it and licking it with its forked tongues.

As soon as I was sure that nothing could save the cottage, I left the scene and sought refuge in the woods.

Now, with the world ahead of me, where should I go? I decided to flee far from the place of my misfortunes, but as someone hated and despised, every country seemed equally terrifying. Then, I thought of you. I learned from your documents that you were my father, my creator, and who better to turn to than the one who had given me life? From the lessons Felix had taught Safie, I had learned about geography, including the locations of different countries. You had mentioned Geneva as your hometown, and I decided to head in that direction.

But how would I navigate? I knew I had to travel southwest to reach my destination, and the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns I would pass through, and I couldn't ask anyone for information. However, I didn't lose hope. My only chance for help was you, even though I felt nothing but hatred towards you. You had given me the ability to perceive and feel, and then you had abandoned me, leaving me to face the scorn and horror of humanity.

old_rewritten_text:
A significant change had taken place in me; my health, which had been declining, was now much improved, and my mood, when not weighed down by the memory of my unhappy promise, had lifted accordingly. My father noticed this change with pleasure and began thinking about how to eliminate the remaining traces of my melancholy, which would still resurface from time to time, casting a dark shadow over the approaching happiness. During these moments, I would seek refuge in complete solitude. I spent entire days alone on the lake in a small boat, watching the clouds and listening to the gentle lapping of the waves, silent and lethargic. However, the fresh air and bright sunshine usually managed to restore me to some degree of calmness, and when I returned, I greeted my friends with a more genuine smile and a more cheerful heart.

After one of these solo outings, my father called me aside and said, 'I'm happy to see, my dear son, that you've started enjoying your old hobbies again and seem to be getting back to yourself. Yet, you still seem unhappy and avoid spending time with us. For a while, I was puzzled about the reason for this, but yesterday an idea occurred to me, and if it's correct, I urge you to be honest about it. Keeping this to yourself would not only be pointless but could also bring triple the misery to all of us.'

I trembled violently at his words, and my father continued, 'I confess, my son, that I've always looked forward to your marriage to our dear Elizabeth as the key to our family's happiness and the comfort of my later years. You two have been close since childhood; you studied together and seemed to have similar personalities and interests. However, human experience can be misleading, and what I thought would bring us together may have actually driven you apart. Perhaps you see Elizabeth as just a sister, without any desire to marry her. Or maybe you've met someone else you love, and feeling obligated to Elizabeth, this inner conflict could be causing the intense pain you seem to be feeling.'

'My dear father, please don't worry,' I replied. 'I love my cousin Elizabeth deeply and sincerely. I've never met anyone who inspires my warmest admiration and affection like she does. My future hopes and dreams are entirely tied to the prospect of us being together.'

'The way you feel about this, my dear Victor, brings me more joy than I've felt in a long time,' my father said. 'If you truly feel this way, we'll definitely be happy, no matter how difficult things seem right now. But it's this sadness that seems to have such a strong hold on you that I want to help you overcome. So, tell me, do you object to getting married soon? We've had some tough times lately, and recent events have disrupted the peaceful life that's suitable for someone of my age and health. You're younger, and I don't think an early marriage would interfere with any future plans you may have for your career or personal growth, considering you have a stable financial situation.'

We visited the tomb of the renowned Hampden and the site where the patriot fell. For a moment, my spirit was lifted from its degrading and miserable fears to contemplate the profound concepts of freedom and self-sacrifice that these sights represented. I momentarily dared to break free from my constraints and look around me with a sense of liberation and a lofty spirit, but the emotional pain had taken its toll, and I sank back into my miserable state, trembling and hopeless.

We left Oxford with regret and headed to Matlock, our next destination. The surrounding countryside resembled the scenery of Switzerland, but on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the majestic backdrop of distant white Alps that always accompanied the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We explored the incredible cave and the small natural history exhibits, where the curiosities were displayed in a similar manner to those in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry mentioned the latter name, I trembled, and I quickly wanted to leave Matlock, as it was now associated with that horrific scene.

From Derby, we continued our journey north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I almost felt like I was back in the Swiss mountains. The remaining patches of snow on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all familiar and dear to me. We also made some acquaintances who almost managed to bring me happiness. Clerval's delight was even greater than mine; his mind thrived in the company of talented individuals, and he discovered greater potential within himself than he thought he possessed when he was surrounded by people who were inferior to him. 'I could spend my life here,' he said to me, 'and among these mountains, I would hardly miss Switzerland and the Rhine.'

But he realized that a traveler's life is one that involves a lot of pain amidst its pleasures. A traveler's emotions are always on edge, and when they start to relax, they have to leave the things that bring them joy to experience something new, which in turn captures their attention, only to be abandoned for other novelties.

We had barely visited the various lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and formed a connection with some of the locals when our scheduled meeting with our Scottish friend approached, and we had to leave. For my part, I wasn't sorry to go. I had neglected my promise for some time, and I feared the consequences of disappointing the demon. He might still be in Switzerland, seeking revenge on my family. This thought haunted me and tormented me at every moment, depriving me of any potential rest and peace. I anxiously awaited my letters, and if they were delayed, I was miserable and overwhelmed by a thousand fears. When the letters arrived, and I saw that they were from Elizabeth or my father, I hardly dared to read them and discover my fate. Sometimes I thought that the monster was following me and might hasten my punishment by killing my companion.

old_rewritten_text:
I climbed up the shed and snuck into my window just before dawn. My new clothes were all stained and muddy, and I was exhausted. 

Well, I got a good scolding from old Miss Watson in the morning because of my clothes, but the widow didn't yell at me. Instead, she just cleaned off the stains and mud, and looked so sorry for me that I thought I'd try to behave for a while if I could. Then Miss Watson took me into the closet and prayed, but nothing came of it. She told me to pray every day and that I'd get whatever I asked for. But that wasn't true. I tried it once and got a fishing line, but no hooks. It was useless to me without hooks. I tried praying for the hooks a few times, but somehow I just couldn't make it work. One day, I asked Miss Watson to try praying for me, but she said I was foolish. She never told me why, and I couldn't figure it out.

I sat down in the woods one time and thought about it for a long time. I said to myself, if you can get anything you pray for, why can't Deacon Winn get back the money he lost on pork? Why can't the widow get back her stolen silver snuffbox? Why can't Miss Watson lose some weight? No, I said to myself, there's nothing to it. I went and told the widow about it, and she said the thing you can get by praying for it is 'spiritual gifts.' This was too much for me to understand, but she explained that it means I should help other people, do everything I can for them, look out for them all the time, and never think about myself. This included Miss Watson, as I understood it. I went out into the woods and thought about it for a long time, but I couldn't see any advantage to it, except for the other people. So, I decided I wouldn't worry about it anymore and just let it go. Sometimes the widow would take me aside and talk about Providence in a way that made my mouth water, but maybe the next day Miss Watson would take over and knock it all down again. I figured I could see that there were two different Providences, and a poor guy would have a pretty good chance with the widow's Providence, but if Miss Watson's got him, there was no hope for him. I thought it all through, and I decided I'd rather belong to the widow's side if I had to choose, though I couldn't figure out how it would make me any better off than I was before, considering how ignorant and low-down I was.

My dad hadn't been seen for over a year, and that was a relief for me. I didn't want to see him anymore. He used to always beat me when he was sober and could catch me, though I usually ran into the woods when he was around. Well, around this time, he was found drowned in the river, about twelve miles upstream from town, or so people said.

I just expected someone would be hiding in it, because people often did that to trick others, and when someone had pulled a small boat out most of the way, they'd jump up and laugh. But that wasn't the case this time. It was definitely a drift canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought to myself, the old man will be happy when he sees this - it's worth about ten dollars. But when I got to shore, my dad wasn't in sight yet, and as I was pulling the canoe into a small creek lined with vines and willows, I had another idea: I figured I'd hide it well, and instead of running into the woods when I took off, I'd go down the river about fifty miles and set up camp in one place for good, and not have such a tough time walking on foot.

It was pretty close to our shack, and I thought I heard my dad coming all the time, but I managed to hide the canoe; then I went out and looked around a bunch of willows, and there was my dad down the path a ways, taking aim at a bird with his gun. So he hadn't seen anything.

When he came along, I was busy pulling in a fishing line. He scolded me a bit for being so slow, but I told him I fell into the river, and that's what made me so late. I knew he'd see that I was wet, and then he'd start asking questions. We caught five catfish on the lines and headed home.

While we were resting after breakfast, both of us being pretty exhausted, I started thinking that if I could come up with a way to keep my dad and the widow from trying to follow me, it would be more reliable than just relying on luck to get far enough away before they missed me; you see, all sorts of things could happen. Well, I didn't see a way to do it for a while, but then my dad sat up for a minute to drink some water, and he said:

'Next time someone comes snooping around here, you wake me up, got it? That guy wasn't here for any good reason. I would've shot him. Next time you wake me up, you hear?'

Then he lay back down and went to sleep again, but what he had said gave me the idea I needed. I thought to myself, I can make it work now so nobody will think of following me.

Around twelve o'clock, we got up and went along the riverbank. The river was rising pretty quickly, and a lot of driftwood was floating by. After a while, a log raft came by - nine logs tied together. We went out in the skiff and towed it to shore. Then we had dinner. Anyone but my dad would've waited out the day to catch more stuff, but that wasn't his style. Nine logs were enough for one time; he had to head straight to town and sell them. So he locked me in and took the skiff, and started off towing the raft around three thirty. I figured he wouldn't be back that night.

Every night, I'd sneak ashore around ten o'clock in some small village and buy ten or fifteen cents' worth of food, like meal, bacon, or other stuff. Sometimes I'd grab a chicken that wasn't roosting comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said, 'Take a chicken when you get the chance, because if you don't want it yourself, you can easily find someone who does, and a good deed is never forgotten.' I never saw Pap when he didn't want the chicken himself, but that's what he always said, anyway.

In the mornings, before daylight, I'd slip into cornfields and take a watermelon, a mushmelon, a pumpkin, or some fresh corn. Pap always said it wasn't harmful to borrow things if you planned to pay them back someday. However, the widow said it was just a nice way of saying stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right, so he suggested we pick a few things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore. Then, he figured it wouldn't be harmful to borrow the rest. We discussed it one night, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to stop taking watermelons, cantaloupes, or mushmelons. By dawn, we had it all settled and decided to stop taking crabapples and persimmons. We weren't feeling great before that, but now we were comfortable. I was glad about the decision, too, because crabapples are never good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for a couple of months yet.

We'd occasionally shoot a bird that got up too early in the morning or didn't go to bed early enough in the evening. Overall, we were living pretty well.

On the fifth night below St. Louis, we had a big storm after midnight, with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain poured down in a solid sheet. We stayed in the wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. When the lightning flashed, we could see a straight river ahead and high, rocky bluffs on both sides. I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had run aground on a rock. We were drifting straight towards it. The lightning showed it very clearly. The boat was leaning over, with part of its upper deck above water, and you could see every little chimney and a chair by the big bell, with an old hat hanging on the back of it, when the lightning flashed.

Well, it being late at night and stormy, and all so mysterious, I felt just like any other boy would when I saw that wreck lying there, so mournful and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to get on board and sneak around a bit, to see what was there. So I said, 'Let's land on it, Jim.'

But Jim was strongly against it at first. He said, 'I don't want to go fooling around any wreck.'

I said.

Oh man, it was out before I could even think about it. And before I could react, she threw her arms around my neck and told me to say it again, say it again, say it again.

I realized I had spoken too quickly and said too much, and I was in a tough spot. I asked her to give me a minute to think, and she sat there, very impatient and excited, but also looking kind of happy and relieved, like someone who's just gotten a painful tooth pulled out. So I started thinking it through. I thought to myself, I guess someone who tells the truth when they're in a tight spot is taking a big risk, although I've never been in a situation like this before and can't say for sure, but it seems that way to me, anyway. And yet, here's a case where it seems to me like the truth is actually better and safer than a lie. I need to remember this and think about it some more, it's so unusual and unexpected. I've never seen anything like it. Well, I finally thought, I'm going to take a chance and tell the truth this time, even though it feels like I'm sitting on a keg of dynamite and lighting the fuse just to see what happens. Then I said:

'Miss Mary Jane, is there a place just outside of town where you could go and stay for a few days?'

'Yes, Mr. Lothrop's. Why?'

'Don't worry about that right now. If I tell you how I know the slaves will see each other again within two weeks, right here in this house, and I can prove it, will you go to Mr. Lothrop's and stay for four days?'

'Four days!' she said. 'I'll stay a year!'

Then I came back and sat down again, and said:

'Don't freak out. Just sit still and take it like an adult. I have to tell you the truth, and you need to be prepared, Miss Mary, because it's going to be tough to hear, but there's no way around it. And then she jumped up, her face on fire with anger, and said:

'That monster! Come on, let's not waste a minute - not a second. We'll have them tarred and feathered and thrown in the river!'

He was oblivious to the stillness that had fallen. 
Dorian Gray suddenly exclaimed, “Basil, I’m exhausted from standing. I need to go out into the garden. The air in here is suffocating.” 
Basil Hallward apologized, “My dear fellow, I’m so sorry. When I’m painting, I become completely absorbed in my work. But you posed perfectly. You remained absolutely still, and I captured the effect I was aiming for – the slightly parted lips and the bright, inquisitive look in your eyes. I don’t know what Harry has been saying to you, but he has certainly inspired a remarkable expression. I suppose he has been flattering you. You shouldn’t take anything he says too seriously.” 
Dorian Gray replied, “He hasn’t been flattering me at all. Perhaps that’s why I don’t believe a word he’s told me.” 
Lord Henry looked at him with his characteristic dreamy, languid eyes and said, “You know you believe every word, though.” He then suggested, “I’ll join you in the garden. It’s terribly hot in the studio. Basil, let’s have something cold to drink, perhaps something with strawberries.” 
Basil Hallward agreed, “Of course, Harry. Just ring the bell, and when Parker arrives, I’ll let him know what you’d like. I need to finish working on this background, so I’ll join you later. Don’t keep Dorian out too long. I’ve never been in better form for painting than I am today. This is going to be my masterpiece, even in its current state.” 
Lord Henry went out to the garden, where he found Dorian Gray with his face buried in the fragrant lilac blossoms, inhaling their scent as if it were intoxicating. He approached Dorian and placed a hand on his shoulder, saying, “You’re doing exactly the right thing. The only way to soothe the soul is through the senses, just as the only way to soothe the senses is through the soul.” 
Dorian started and pulled back, his eyes wide with a frightened look, as if he had been suddenly awakened. His nostrils flared, and a hidden nerve caused his lips to tremble. 
Lord Henry continued, “Yes, that’s one of life’s great secrets – to find solace for the soul through the senses, and for the senses through the soul. You’re an extraordinary young man. You know more than you think you do, yet you know less than you want to.” 
Dorian Gray looked away, frowning. He couldn’t help but be drawn to the tall, elegant young man standing beside him. Lord Henry’s romantic, olive-skinned face and weary expression fascinated him. His low, languid voice was captivating, and even his cool, white hands seemed to have a charm of their own, moving like music as he spoke. However, Dorian felt a sense of fear and shame at being afraid. Why had it taken a stranger to reveal his true self to him? He had known Basil Hallward for months, but their friendship had never had a profound impact on him. Now, someone had entered his life, and it seemed as though this person had uncovered the mystery of life for him.
