“Don’t go to the theater tonight, Dorian,” said Hallward. “Stay and have dinner with me.”

“I can’t, Basil.”

“Why not?”

“Because I promised Lord Henry Wotton I’d go with him.”

“He won’t think more of you for keeping your promises. He always breaks his own. I'm begging you, don’t go.”

Dorian Gray laughed and shook his head.

“Please, I'm asking you.”

The young man hesitated, glancing over at Lord Henry, who was watching them from the coffee table with an amused smile.

“I have to go, Basil,” he replied.

“Fine,” said Hallward, and he got up and put his cup on the tray. “It's getting late, and since you need to get dressed, you should probably get going. Goodbye, Harry. Goodbye, Dorian. Come see me soon. How about tomorrow?”

“Definitely.”

“Don’t forget, okay?”

“No, of course not,” Dorian said.

“And, Harry!”

“Yes, Basil?”

“Remember what I asked you when we were in the garden this morning?”

“I forgot.”

“I trust you.”

“I wish I could trust myself,” Lord Henry said with a laugh. “Come on, Mr. Gray, my car is outside, and I can drop you off at your place. Goodbye, Basil. It's been a really interesting afternoon.”

As the door closed behind them, the painter threw himself down on a couch, and a look of pain crossed his face.


At 12:30 the next day, Lord Henry Wotton strolled from Curzon Street to the Albany to visit his uncle, Lord Fermor, a genial but somewhat rough-around-the-edges old bachelor. The outside world considered him selfish because they didn't benefit from him, but Society thought he was generous because he entertained the people who amused him. His father had been the ambassador to Madrid when Isabella was young and Prim was unknown, but he had quit the diplomatic service on a whim when he wasn't offered the embassy in Paris, a position he felt he deserved due to his birth, his laid-back attitude, his clear writing style, and his love of pleasure. The son, who had been his father's secretary, had resigned along with his boss, which was seen as a foolish move at the time. After inheriting the title a few months later, he dedicated himself to mastering the art of doing absolutely nothing. He owned two large townhouses but preferred to live in a smaller place because it was less hassle, and he usually ate at his club. He paid some attention to managing his coal mines in the Midlands, justifying this bit of work by saying that having coal allowed him to afford the luxury of burning wood in his own fireplace. In politics, he was a conservative, except when the conservatives were in power, at which point he would strongly criticize them for being too liberal. He was a hero to his valet, who bossed him around, and he intimidated most of his relatives, whom he bullied in turn. Only a country like England could have produced someone like him, and he always said that the country was going downhill. His principles were outdated, but there was something to be said for his biases.

“They go to America,” Lord Henry murmured.

Sir Thomas frowned. “I'm afraid your nephew is biased against that great country,” he said to Lady Agatha. “I've traveled all over it, and the people who hosted me were extremely courteous. I can tell you, it's really eye-opening to visit.”

“But do we really need to see Chicago to be educated?” Mr. Erskine asked, sounding a bit exasperated. “I don't feel up to the trip.”

Sir Thomas waved his hand dismissively. “Mr. Erskine has the world at his fingertips, but we practical people like to experience things firsthand, not just read about them. The Americans are a fascinating people. They're extremely pragmatic. I think that's what sets them apart. Yes, Mr. Erskine, they're a very pragmatic people. I assure you, there's no pretension about the Americans.”

“How dreadful!” Lord Henry exclaimed. “I can handle aggression, but unrelenting logic is unbearable. There's something unfair about using it. It's like cheating intellectually.”

“I don't understand what you mean,” Sir Thomas said, his face reddening.

“I think I do, Lord Henry,” Mr. Erskine said with a smile.

“Paradoxes are all well and good, but...” Sir Thomas began.

“Was that a paradox?” Mr. Erskine asked. “I didn't think so. Maybe it was. The thing about paradoxes is that they can reveal the truth. To really understand reality, we need to see it from different angles. When we challenge our assumptions, we can judge what's real.”

“Oh dear, you men and your arguments!” Lady Agatha said. “I never know what you're talking about. Oh, Harry, I'm so frustrated with you. Why are you trying to convince Mr. Dorian Gray to give up his work in the East End? I'm sure he'd be invaluable to them. They'd love his music.”

“I want him to play for me,” Lord Henry said, smiling, and he caught a bright, answering glance from across the table.

“But the people in Whitechapel are so unhappy,” Lady Agatha continued.

“I can empathize with anything except suffering,” Lord Henry said, shrugging. “I just can't relate to it. It's too ugly, too horrific, too distressing. There's something morbid about the way people obsess over pain these days. We should be focusing on the beauty, the joy of life. The less said about life's problems, the better.”

“Still, the East End is a major issue,” Sir Thomas said, shaking his head gravely.

“Absolutely,” the young lord replied. “It's a problem of oppression, and we try to solve it by entertaining the oppressed.”

The politician looked at him intently. “What's your proposed solution, then?” he asked.

Lord Henry laughed. “I don't want to change anything in England except the weather,” he said. “I'm happy to just think about these things. But since the nineteenth century has been bankrupted by excessive sentimentality, I think we should look to science for answers. The good thing about emotions is that they can lead us astray, and the good thing about science is that it's not emotional.”

“But we have such serious responsibilities,” Mrs. Vandeleur ventured, sounding timid.

“Very serious,” Lady Agatha echoed.

He was supposed to get off the ship in Melbourne, say goodbye to the captain, and head to the gold fields right away. Within a week, he would find a huge nugget of gold, the biggest one ever discovered, and bring it back to the coast in a wagon guarded by six police officers on horses. However, outlaws would try to attack them three times, and they would be defeated with many of the outlaws being killed. Or maybe he wouldn't go to the gold fields at all. They were terrible places where men got drunk, shot each other in bars, and used bad language. Instead, he would be a nice sheep farmer, and one evening, while riding home, he would see a beautiful heiress being taken away by a robber on a black horse. He would chase after them and rescue her. Of course, she would fall in love with him, and he with her, and they would get married and live in a huge house in London. Yes, great things were waiting for him. But he had to be good, not lose his temper, and not waste his money. She was only a year older than him, but she knew much more about life. He had to remember to write to her every chance he got and say his prayers every night before bed. God was good and would watch over him. She would pray for him too, and in a few years, he would come back rich and happy.

The boy listened to her with a scowl and didn't say a word. He was very sad about leaving home. But that wasn't the only reason he was gloomy. Even though he was young, he knew that Sibyl was in a dangerous situation. The rich young man who was in love with her didn't have good intentions. He was a gentleman, and the boy hated him for that. He hated him because of a strong feeling that he couldn't explain, and that feeling was even stronger because he didn't understand it. He also knew that his mother was shallow and selfish, and he saw a lot of danger for Sibyl in that. Children love their parents when they're young, but as they grow up, they start to judge them. Sometimes they forgive them.

His mother! He had something important to ask her, something he had been thinking about for months. Something he had heard at the theater, a whispered insult that had reached his ears one night as he waited at the stage door, had started a chain of terrible thoughts. He remembered it like a whip hitting his face. His eyebrows came together in a deep frown, and he bit his lip in pain.

"You're not listening to a word I'm saying, Jim," Sibyl said, "and I'm making wonderful plans for your future. Say something."

"What do you want me to say?" he asked.

"Oh, that you'll be a good boy and not forget us," she replied, smiling at him.

He shrugged his shoulders. "You're more likely to forget me than I am to forget you, Sibyl."

I have to go now. Goodbye. Don't forget that you'll only have one child to take care of from now on, and I'm warning you, if this man hurts my sister, I'll find out who he is and make him pay. I'm dead serious about it.

The over-the-top threat, the passionate gesture that went with it, and the dramatic words made life feel more intense to her. She was used to this kind of atmosphere. She felt more at ease, and for the first time in months, she genuinely admired her son. She would have loved to keep the scene going on the same emotional level, but he cut her off. They had to get the luggage downstairs and find their scarves. The hotel staff were rushing in and out, and there was the hassle of negotiating with the taxi driver. The moment was lost in mundane details. As she waved goodbye from the window, watching her son drive away, she felt a renewed sense of disappointment. She tried to console herself by telling Sibyl how empty her life would feel now that she only had one child to look after. She remembered the phrase and it had struck a chord with her. As for the threat, she didn't mention it. It was a vivid and dramatic expression, and she felt that they would all laugh about it someday.

That evening, Lord Henry said to Basil, "I suppose you've heard the news?" as Hallward was shown into a private room at the Bristol, where dinner was set for three.

"No, Harry," the artist replied, handing his hat and coat to the waiter. "What's going on? I hope it's not about politics. They don't interest me. There's hardly anyone in parliament worth painting, although a lot of them could use a makeover."

"Dorian Gray is engaged to be married," Lord Henry said, watching Basil's reaction.

Hallward was taken aback and then frowned. "Dorian engaged to be married? That's impossible!" he exclaimed.

"It's true," Lord Henry said.

"To whom?" Hallward asked.

"To some young actress or other," Lord Henry replied.

"I don't believe it. Dorian's too sensible for that," Hallward said.

"Dorian's also wise enough to do foolish things from time to time, my dear Basil," Lord Henry said with a smile.

"Marriage is a big commitment, Harry. It's not something you can just do on a whim," Hallward said.

"Unless you're in America, perhaps," Lord Henry said lazily. "But I didn't say he was married. I said he's engaged. There's a big difference. I vaguely recall being married, but I don't remember ever being engaged. I'm starting to think I never was."

"Think about Dorian's background, his social status, and his wealth. It would be crazy for him to marry someone so far beneath him," Hallward said.

"If you want to make sure Dorian marries this girl, just tell him that, Basil. He's bound to do the opposite. Whenever a man does something really stupid, it's always for the noblest reasons," Lord Henry said.

"I hope the girl is a good person, Harry. I don't want to see Dorian tied down to someone who might ruin his life and destroy his intellect," Hallward said.

"Oh, she's more than just good – she's beautiful," Lord Henry murmured, sipping his drink.

“The only thing worth having a theory about is pleasure,” he replied in his smooth, melodious voice. “But I don't think I can claim this theory as my own. It's more about human nature than anything else. Pleasure is a sign that we're doing something right. When we're happy, we're usually good, but being good doesn't always mean we're happy.”

“Wait, what do you mean by good?” asked Basil Hallward.

“Yes, what do you mean by good, Harry?” Dorian echoed, leaning back in his chair and looking at Lord Henry over the vibrant purple flowers in the center of the table.

Things like that can make someone a celebrity in Paris, but in London, people are so judgmental. Here, you should never start out with a scandal. You should save that for later in life to make your older years more interesting. I'm guessing they don't know your name at the theater, which is a good thing. Did anyone see you going to her room? That's a crucial point.

Dorian didn't respond for a few moments. He was shocked and horrified. Finally, he stuttered, in a barely audible voice, 'Harry, what did you mean by an inquest? Was it an accident? Oh, Harry, I just can't handle it. Tell me everything right now.'

'I'm sure it wasn't an accident, Dorian, although that's what we'll have to tell the public,' Harry said. 'Apparently, as she was leaving the theater with her mom around 12:30, she said she had forgotten something upstairs. They waited for a while, but she never came back down. Eventually, they found her lying dead on the floor of her dressing room. She had ingested something by mistake, some toxic substance they use in theaters. I'm not sure what it was, but it had either cyanide or lead in it. I think it was probably cyanide, since she seemed to have died instantly.'

'Harry, this is terrible!' the young man exclaimed.

'Yes, it's very tragic, of course, but you can't let it get to you. I saw in the news that she was seventeen. I would have thought she was even younger than that. She looked like a kid and seemed to know so little about acting. Dorian, you can't let this get to you. You should come and have dinner with me, and then we'll go to the opera. It's a big night, and everyone will be there. You can join me in my sister's box. She's got some interesting women with her.'

'I've basically murdered Sibyl Vane,' Dorian Gray said to himself, 'killed her just as surely as if I had cut her throat with a knife. And yet, the roses are just as beautiful, and the birds are singing just as happily in my garden. But I wasn't moved at all.

The moment she became a part of real life, she damaged it, and it damaged her, and so she disappeared. You can mourn Ophelia if you want. Wear ashes on your head because Cordelia was murdered. Protest against fate because the daughter of Brabantio died. But don't waste your tears on Sibyl Vane. She was less real than they are."

There was a silence. The evening grew darker in the room. Silently, and with an eerie presence, the shadows crept in from the garden. The colors faded slowly out of everything.

After a while, Dorian Gray looked up. "You've helped me understand myself, Harry," he murmured with a sigh of relief. "I felt everything you've said, but somehow I was afraid of it, and I couldn't express it to myself. You know me so well. But we won't talk about what's happened again. It's been an incredible experience. That's all. I wonder if life has anything else in store for me that's just as amazing."

"Life has everything in store for you, Dorian," Lord Henry said. "With your extraordinary good looks, there's nothing you won't be able to do."

"But what if I become old and wrinkled, Harry? What then?"

"Then, my dear Dorian," Lord Henry said, standing up to leave, "you'd have to fight for your successes. As it is, they're handed to you. No, you have to keep your good looks. We live in an age that overthinks everything and values knowledge over beauty. We can't afford to lose you. Now, you should get dressed and meet me at the club. We're running late."

"I think I'll join you at the opera, Harry. I'm too tired to eat. What's the number of your sister's box?"

"It's twenty-seven, I think. It's on the grand tier. You'll see her name on the door. But I'm sorry you won't come and dine with us."

"I don't feel up to it," Dorian said listlessly. "But thanks for everything you've said to me. You're definitely my best friend. No one has ever understood me like you have."

"We're just starting our friendship, Dorian," Lord Henry replied, shaking his hand. "Goodbye. I'll see you before nine-thirty, I hope. Remember, Patti is performing."

As he closed the door behind him, Dorian Gray rang the bell, and soon Victor appeared with the lamps and closed the blinds. Dorian waited impatiently for him to leave. The man seemed to take forever to do everything.

As soon as he was gone, Dorian rushed to the screen and pulled it back. No, there was no further change in the picture. It had already reflected the news of Sibyl Vane's death before Dorian had even known about it himself. It was aware of the events of life as they happened. The cruel twist that marred the fine lines of the mouth had probably appeared the moment the girl had taken the poison, whatever it was. Or was it indifferent to the consequences? Did it simply acknowledge what was happening within the soul? Dorian wondered, and he hoped that one day he would see the change happen before his eyes, shuddering at the thought.

As morning breaks, white fingers of light creep through the curtains, and they seem to tremble. Dark, fantastical shapes - silent shadows - crawl into the corners of the room and huddle there. Outside, the sounds of birds chirping among the leaves, people heading to work, or the wind sighing and sobbing as it comes down from the hills and circles the silent house, are all audible. It's as if the wind is hesitant to wake the sleepers, yet it must rouse sleep from its deep, purple slumber. Veil after veil of thin, dusky gauze lifts, and gradually, the forms and colors of things are restored to them. We watch as dawn recreates the world in its timeless pattern. The pale mirrors regain their reflective life. The unlit candles stand where we had left them, and beside them lies the half-read book we had been studying, or the wired flower we had worn to the ball, or the letter we had been afraid to read, or the one we had read too many times. Nothing appears to have changed. The real life we knew returns from the unreal shadows of the night, and we must resume it where we left off. A terrible sense of the necessity for continuing our routine, with its monotonous, stereotyped habits, washes over us. Alternatively, we may feel a wild longing for our eyes to open one morning to a world that has been transformed in the darkness, a world with fresh shapes and colors, where things would be changed, or hold new secrets. In this world, the past would have little or no place, or would survive only as a subconscious memory, without the burden of obligation or regret. Even the recollection of joy would be bitter, and memories of pleasure would be painful.

For Dorian Gray, creating such worlds seemed to be the true purpose of life. In his pursuit of new and exciting sensations, with their essential element of strangeness that fuels romance, he would often adopt certain ways of thinking that he knew were not truly his own. He would surrender to their subtle influences, absorb their essence, and then, having satisfied his intellectual curiosity, leave them behind with a curious indifference. This indifference is not incompatible with a genuine ardor of temperament and, according to some modern psychologists, is often a condition of it.

There was a rumor that Dorian Gray was going to join the Roman Catholic Church, and it's true that the Roman ritual had always fascinated him. The daily sacrifice, more awe-inspiring than any ancient sacrifice, moved him deeply. It was the ritual's rejection of sensory evidence, its primitive simplicity, and the eternal pathos of the human tragedy it symbolized that drew him in. He loved to kneel on the cold marble floor and watch the priest, in his ornate, flower-patterned dalmatic, slowly lift the veil of the tabernacle or raise the jeweled, lantern-shaped monstrance with the pale wafer that, at times, seemed to be the true 'bread of angels.' He was also captivated by the priest, robed in the garments of Christ's Passion, breaking the Host into the chalice and striking his breast in penance for his sins.

In his pursuit of new and exciting sensations, with their essential element of strangeness that fuels romance, he would often adopt certain ways of thinking that he knew were not truly his own. He would surrender to their subtle influences, absorb their essence, and then, having satisfied his intellectual curiosity, leave them behind with a curious indifference. This indifference is not incompatible with a genuine ardor of temperament and, according to some modern psychologists, is often a condition of it.

There was a rumor that Dorian Gray was going to join the Roman Catholic Church, and it's true that the Roman ritual had always fascinated him. The daily sacrifice, more awe-inspiring than any ancient sacrifice, moved him deeply. It was the ritual's rejection of sensory evidence, its primitive simplicity, and the eternal pathos of the human tragedy it symbolized that drew him in. He loved to kneel on the cold marble floor and watch the priest, in his ornate, flower-patterned dalmatic, slowly lift the veil of the tabernacle or raise the jeweled, lantern-shaped monstrance with the pale wafer that, at times, seemed to be the true 'bread of angels.' He was also captivated by the priest, robed in the garments of Christ's Passion, breaking the Host into the chalice and striking his breast in penance for his sins.
